title: Human Heart & Double Circulation
summary: Follow oxygen-poor and oxygen-rich blood through the heart's four chambers, valves, and double circulation circuits.
focus: Four chambers, one-way valves, pulmonary and systemic circulation, and the cardiac cycle

cues.text: Hello everyone! Here's a question to begin today's class: your heart is beating right now, while you were sleeping, walking and even when you weren't thinking about it.
Have you ever wondered how it manages to pump blood continuously, and how blood knows where to go?
Today, we're going inside the human heart to understand its four chambers, its valves, two circulation pathways and the fascinating process called the cardiac cycle. Let's begin!
Look carefully at this diagram. The human heart has four chambers: the two upper chambers are called atria, and the two lower chambers are called ventricles.

On the anatomical right side, we have the right atrium and right ventricle. On the anatomical left side, we have the left atrium and left ventricle. Remember, anatomical right and left refer to the person's body, not your viewing direction.
Now, what is the job of these chambers? The atria receive blood entering the heart; the ventricles pump blood out. Here's our first memory trick: Atria receive. Ventricles pump.
Imagine blood entering a chamber and moving forward — we don't want it flowing backwards. The heart solves this problem using four one-way valves.
First, the tricuspid valve between right atrium and ventricle; second, the pulmonary valve between right ventricle and pulmonary artery.

Third, the mitral or bicuspid valve between left atrium and ventricle; fourth, the aortic valve between left ventricle and aorta. Each valve opens to let blood move forward and closes to prevent backflow.
Let's follow the journey of blood: deoxygenated blood returning from the body enters the right atrium through the superior and inferior vena cava.
It moves into the right ventricle, which pumps it through the pulmonary valve and into the pulmonary artery toward the lungs.
Inside the lungs, blood releases carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen. This journey from heart to lungs and back to the heart is called pulmonary circulation: Heart to lungs to heart!
Now the blood is rich in oxygen. It returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins and enters the left atrium, then moves into the left ventricle.
The left ventricle has a particularly thick muscular wall because it must pump blood throughout the entire body past the aortic valve and into the aorta.
The aorta distributes oxygen-rich blood to body tissues. Tissues use the oxygen and nutrients, and blood returns through veins: Systemic circulation serves the whole body!
One complete sequence of contraction and relaxation is called the cardiac cycle. Systole means contraction; diastole means relaxation.
Stage one: atrial systole pushes blood into ventricles. Stage two: ventricular systole pumps to lungs and body as atrioventricular valves snap shut with a lub sound.
Stage three: joint diastole, where both atria and ventricles relax and refill. At 75 bpm, one complete cardiac cycle lasts approximately 0.8 seconds.
Question one: Which chamber pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body? Pause and think. Correct answer: the left ventricle!
Question two: Which circulation carries blood from the heart to the lungs? Correct: Pulmonary circulation.
Question three: Which valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle? That's the mitral, or bicuspid, valve.
Question four: What are the three stages of the cardiac cycle? Atrial systole, ventricular systole, and joint diastole. Excellent!
Let's bring everything together: the human heart has four chambers, one-way valves, pulmonary and systemic circuits, and a continuous cardiac cycle.
Here's your final challenge: without looking at your notes, explain how blood travels from the body to the lungs, returns to the heart and reaches the entire body.
If you can explain that double circulation pathway, you've understood the heart. Great work everyone, see you in the next class!

notes.title: The Four Chambers & One-Way Valves
notes.text: The right side receives deoxygenated blood and pumps to the lungs; the left side receives oxygenated blood and pumps to the body. Four valves (tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, aortic) ensure strictly unidirectional blood flow.

notes.title: Double Circulation: Pulmonary & Systemic
notes.text: Deoxygenated blood travels via vena cava → RA → RV → pulmonary artery → lungs (pulmonary circuit). Oxygenated blood returns via pulmonary veins → LA → LV → aorta → body tissues (systemic circuit).
notes.equation: Pulmonary: Heart → Lungs → Heart · Systemic: Heart → Body → Heart

notes.title: The Cardiac Cycle (0.8s at 75 bpm)
notes.text: One complete heartbeat consists of three phases: atrial systole (atria contract, 0.1s), ventricular systole (ventricles contract, AV valves snap shut 'lub', 0.3s), and joint diastole (all chambers relax and refill, semilunar valves snap shut 'dub', 0.4s).
notes.equation: Cardiac Cycle = Atrial Systole (0.1s) + Ventricular Systole (0.3s) + Joint Diastole (0.4s) = 0.8s

mistake: Don’t assume all arteries carry oxygenated blood and all veins carry deoxygenated blood. Arteries are defined as vessels carrying blood AWAY from the heart, so the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood away from the right ventricle. Veins carry blood TOWARD the heart, so pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood.

practice.question: Why is the myocardial wall of the left ventricle significantly thicker than that of the right ventricle?
practice.answer: The right ventricle only needs to pump blood a short distance to the low-resistance lungs (pulmonary circuit), whereas the left ventricle must generate high systemic pressure to propel blood throughout the entire body (systemic circuit).
